III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00656
First comes the Longitudinal Order of archangels, which forms the “World of the Mothers”: transcendent Lights without any direct relationship to the world disclosed by sensory perception.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00657

Second comes the Latitudinal Order of the theurgic archangels, the archetypal persons or Lords of the Species, of which the Species are images, icons, or theurgic manifestations. One might think that the manner of existence of these two hierarchies, resembling as it does that of the Neoplatonic Dii-Angeli, the God-Angels who mediate the hidden Godhead, differs from that of the angels of the Bible and the Quran.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00658

But such an impression would be entirely foreign to the understanding of the Ishrâqîyûn philosophers. Third and finally come the Angel-Souls: the celestial Souls that move the planetary spheres, and human Souls—the Espahbad Lights.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00659

Several observations should be made here. To begin with, the single order of supreme Intellects or “Cherubim” known to Avicennian philosophy has been divided into two. More precisely, it has unfolded into a double hierarchy whose names and functions were not anticipated by Avicenna: on one side, the “World of the Mothers”; on the other, the “Lords of the Species,” or archetypes.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00660

Secondly, the boundary between the celestial and material worlds is no longer marked, as in Peripatetic philosophy, by the sphere of the Moon. Already the Heaven of the Fixed Stars marks the boundary between the angelic universe of Light (Rûhâbâd) and the universe of the barzakh, the intervening realm. The barzakh is the boundary, the dividing line between the West and the East of being; even the celestial spheres, however subtle their matter, already belong to the West. This was something Avicenna's story of Hayy ibn Yaqzân already understood.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00661

A third observation concerns the transformation undergone here by Zoroastrian angelology. Suhrawardi names all the Amahraspands by their Persian names, and they perform in his theosophy the same roles they perform in Zoroastrian theology. When he identifies the archangel Bahman with the first Intellect proceeding from the Light of Lights, one might therefore expect the other Amahraspands to proceed immediately after him within the “World of the Mothers.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00662

But this is not what happens. Between the archangel Bahman and the Latitudinal Order of archetypes, where Suhrawardi places the names of the other Zoroastrian archangels, lies the Longitudinal Order, the hierarchy of the “World of the Mothers.” The Zoroastrian group of seven—or six—is thus, as it were, stretched apart. No doubt this enlargement was necessary to accommodate hierarchies corresponding to the Neoplatonic Dii-Angeli.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00663

Yet it gives rise to a further consequence. Between the supreme archangels, who are the first Principles or the “World of the Mothers,” and the archetypal archangels, who bear the very names of the Zoroastrian archangels, there exists a relationship of imitation and embodiment comparable to that between a Species and its Angel. The latter archangels arise, in fact, from combinations and exchanges of light occurring in ever-increasing proportions among the supreme archangels.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00664

Should we then speak, in some sense, of archetypes of archetypes? The question remains open, especially because it accords with the Mazdean conception of the Fravartis as heavenly archetypal beings corresponding to all beings of Light. Even the Amahraspands and Ohrmazd himself, as well as the multitude of the Yazdân—the Dii-Angeli—have their Fravarti. The way is open here for meditations that explore.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00665

Finally, the Latitudinal Order of Lights, composed of the Angels of the Species, includes the Angel who is specifically Lord of the human Species, the Angel of humanity (Sâhib tilism al-Nu’ al-nâtiq, Rabb al-Nu’ al-insânî). This is also the Angel of Knowledge and the Angel of Revelation: Gabriel, identified with the Holy Spirit in the Quranic tradition, and with the “Active Intellect” in the philosophical tradition. This figure does not belong to the group of Amahraspands, but shares certain features with the Avestan angel Sraosha (Persian Sorûsh). By incorporating this Angel into the fullness of the archetypal Archangelic Lights, Suhrawardi brings together biblical and Quranic angelology with the angelology of the “Zoroastrian Neoplatonism” of Eastern Theosophy.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00666

The Angel's role as a guide through spiritual initiation is crucial, both in Suhrawardi's writings and in the devotion he personally practiced. We noted above that the way Suhrawardi addresses this Angel as his “Perfect Nature” reveals, at the very least, how he understands the relationship between the Angel of a Species and every individual belonging to it. The same can be said of the other personal liturgies collected in his “Book of Hours.” Any account of his angelology would be incomplete without mentioning them. Their inspiration closely resembles the “Chaldean” spirit of the hymns composed by the Neoplatonist Proclus.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
en-book-2-ch-3-s5
5. Psalms to the Archangel of the Sun and to the “Perfect Nature”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00667
We have already mentioned this group of highly original compositions, which together form something like a “Book of Hours.” Manuscripts are extremely rare, and the text is difficult.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00668

Nevertheless, Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, the great seventeenth-century master of Ishrâqî philosophy, knew these compositions well. In his Glosses on the Book of Eastern Theosophy, he quotes them at length, bearing witness to the persistence, across the centuries, of this liturgical form in which the sacred, ritual devotion of the shaykh al-Ishrâq finds expression. The “Book of Hours” contains, on the one hand, a series of sermons with an eschatological character. Here eschatology concerns the individual's final destiny: the moment when the initiate's soul rises definitively into the world of Light, ascends to its “East,” and thereby disappears from this world, which is its “West.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00669

On the other hand, the “Book of Hours” contains a series of hymns of praise—doxologies—in honor of the Angels of the seven planets. Sadrâ Shîrâzî describes it in terms entirely consistent with what we know of the work: “For each of the seven days of the week, the shaykh al-Ishrâq had a particular hymn of praise in which he celebrated and invoked one of the Seven Angels. Each liturgy contains a hymn followed by a prayer, both so complete that nothing could be added to them.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00670

This “Book of Hours” brings us back to Suhrawardi's fundamental conviction: the perfected mystical theosopher, the hakîm mota’allih, cannot separate philosophical knowledge from spiritual experience. Suhrawardi's “Book of Hours” represents precisely the outcome that Neoplatonic metaphysics found in the theurgic or “hieratic” devotion of the Chaldean Oracles and Orphic hymns—texts that the Neoplatonists interpreted and that, in turn, inspired hymns of their own (above, Chapter II, § 1 onward).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00671

However faithful and exact descriptions of the mystic's sacred experience may be, they remain descriptions. For the experience to be shown in action, to become an event, two paths are open. One is the visionary narrative told in the first person, using mystical symbols; Suhrawardi composed several such accounts (below, Chapters V and VI). The other is prayer, above all what is called monâjât, an intimate psalm in which the person praying addresses another as “you.” Only at this moment is the whole of philosophical knowledge transformed into a divine work, an act of theurgy involving personal spiritual realization.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00672

When a thinker such as Suhrawardi succeeds, on the one hand, in giving form to symbols that are truly his own, and, on the other, in finding the Prayer that only he could have formulated—the “Prayer taught him by his own Perfect Nature,” as the Hermetic tradition would put it—he surely tells us more about himself and about the objective reality of the worlds present to him than a thousand pages of theoretical exposition could ever reveal. Suhrawardi addressed the figures of the heavenly fullness, the Lights of divine beauty glimpsed in fleeting visions, in the language of the “theurgic psalm.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00673

We shall translate two of these psalms below. Here his devotion comes closest to the “hieratic” method of a Neoplatonist such as Proclus, a thinker capable both of the most intricate metaphysical speculation and of composing hymns in honor of the divine beings to whom his personal devotion was directed. Suhrawardi, for his part, knew that he stood in profound harmony with the tradition of the ancient Sages of Persia and Chaldea.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00674

He makes this especially clear when he recalls why these sages and theosophers revered the Flame. Just as every species is the theurgic manifestation and image of one of the Victorious Lights, a Light from which it proceeds and by which it is governed, so Fire—meaning luminous Fire (nâr dhat al-nûr), not the fire of Hell—is the theurgic manifestation of the archangel Ordîbehesht, one of the seven Amahraspands, called Arta Vahishta in Avestan.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00675

As we have already seen, motion and heat are forms in which Light manifests itself (mazhar); they have no cause other than Light. Nowhere do motion and heat reach a higher degree than in Fire. Fire is closest to life, and it is a defense against Darkness. Far from being simply one of the four elements of classical physics, it is “the brother of the human Espahbad Light.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00676

Thus, if the human soul is entrusted with a greater khalifat, a greater vicegerency or delegated spiritual authority in this world, Fire assumes a lesser khalifat as the representative of the celestial Lights in the world of bodies, or barzakh.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00677

What is honored in Fire, therefore, is the image and particular theurgic manifestation of one of the Archangelic Lights. Because Fire performs in our world the same function of revealing a higher reality that the invisible Lights perform in the higher worlds, the ancient Persians had every reason to take the Flame as the qibla, the point toward which they turned in prayer. Suhrawardi's commentators recall the liturgical institutions attributed to the rulers of ancient Iran—Hûshang, Jamshîd, Fereydûn, and Kay Khosraw—and finally given their definitive form by the sage Zoroaster.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00678

Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî understood this perfectly. In the Gloss cited above, he emphasizes that the ancient Persians took the Flame as the qibla of their religious services because “they called the Flame the daughter of the sun (bint al-shams). For them, therefore, it was like the sun's representative or deputy (nâ’ib), by virtue of the strength of its being and its manifestation at every time and in every place, even when the sun was absent, just as the Moon represents the sun at certain times during the night.” This account of the veneration of the Flame thus provides a natural transition to the texts in which Suhrawardi gives us more than a mere echo of ancient solar theologies. What we hear is a psalm whose whole character is shaped by his “Eastern Theosophy.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00679

Nothing in the starry universe is dead or inert, for every Sphere is governed and animated by a thinking Soul. That Soul communicates its energy through the heavenly body set within its Sphere, which serves as its principal organ, its heart. Through this organ, the energies received from the Anima caelestis, the celestial Soul, flow into the sensible world.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00680

So it is with the Sun, which Suhrawardi calls by its Iranian name, Hûrakhsh (Sol splendidus, the splendid Sun), and which the Avesta greets as “the most beautiful manifestation of Ohrmazd.” Suhrawardi describes it as the theurgic manifestation of the archangel Shahrîvar, one of the seven Amahraspands—the Avestan Xshathra Vairya, “Desirable Dominion,” whom the Avesta specifically describes as “having the appearance of the sun.” In Suhrawardi's hierarchy of Archangelic Lights, Shahrîvar belongs to the Latitudinal Order of archetypes. The Ishrâqî tradition, the tradition of the “Eastern” theosophers, therefore gives special honor to this brilliantly shining heavenly body, the “bringer of Day and prince of Heaven.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00681
The reference here to the “Eastern” theosophers has a precise purpose. The Sun's incandescent mass is certainly marvelous, and the continuation of life on Earth depends upon its radiance.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00682

But Suhrawardi has something more fundamental in mind: everything implied, for him, by the notions of “East” and “rising Sun” (above, Chapter II, § 2). There is a way of perceiving sensible things simultaneously in this world and in the malakût, the invisible spiritual world: of perceiving, together with the Sun of this world, the spiritual Sun of the world beyond the senses. What matters to “Eastern Theosophy” is the rising of that spiritual Sun. This is the meaning suggested by a lengthy passage in the Book of Crossroads and Conversations, indispensable for understanding the psalm translated below.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00683

Suhrawardi explains there that, were it not for the obstacle of the material body, our souls would receive the impressions of knowledge directly from the celestial Souls, the Animae caelestes. He then mentions certain inferior practices of divination that have nothing to do with the spiritual elite. This is the same distinction that the “Chaldean Magi” insisted upon between the wise practitioners of theurgy and those engaged in sorcery.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00684

As for the “hieratic” sages, both their knowledge and their spiritual practices are “expressed in symbols” (marmûza), some of which are to be found in his Book of Eastern Theosophy. He goes on to describe the ways in which an encounter with invisible realities (al-amr al-ghaybî) may occur: sometimes as though one were reading a written text; sometimes through hearing the voice of an unseen speaker, a voice that may sound sweet or terrifying, or may be no more than a faint rustling.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00685

At other times, the speaker appears in a visible form. This may be a figure associated with the stars, or one of the heavenly Princes manifesting in a form suited to the visionary's spiritual state. Such experiences are always real events, although they do not take place in our ordinary world, but in the mystical world of Hûrqalyâ, the mundus imaginalis, or “intermediate East.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00686

Suhrawardi then adds: “The gateway (pîshgâh) to all authentic ecstasies in the mystical world of Hûrqalyâ is precisely that of the magnificent Lord Hûrakhsh, the most magnificent of beings who have assumed a material body (motajassidîn), the Most Venerated, who is the supreme Face of God in the language of Eastern Theosophy, the language of Ishrâq. For he is the one who watches over meditation by dispensing light to it, and who is its witness in contemplation.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00687

These explanations make it clear that we are dealing with something other than the physical star, the incandescent mass of the Sun perceived by our ordinary senses. When the psalm translated below addresses Lord Hûrakhsh, the “gateway” to ecstasy, as “the most luminous of beings endowed with life and thought,” and speaks of “the splendor of his thinking soul,” it is unmistakably addressing a higher spiritual being. The entire psalm calls to mind the text known as the “Liturgy of Mithra,” which is actually less a liturgy than a personal rite of initiation, the celebration of a mysterion, a sacrament of immortality.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00688

We know that in the Avesta, Mithra is the lord of heavenly Light and therefore of all the heavenly lights. Neither in the mysteries bearing his name nor in the Avesta is Mithra himself the Sun; rather, the Sun is his chariot. In Suhrawardi's psalm, the hymn of praise celebrates the “body of light” of Lord Hûrakhsh, while the invocation addresses him as the thinking Soul of that luminous body. The scheme of angelology described above is thus confirmed.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00689

Addressing Lord Hûrakhsh, the psalm asks him in turn to pray to his “father,” the one who causes “his thinking soul to rise at its East,” that is, in the heaven of Hûrqalyâ. The Sun's incandescent mass is indeed the theurgic manifestation, the form through which the archangel Shahrîvar becomes visible. The Anima caelestis governing that mass, the Soul “moved by the ardor of love,” is Lord Hûrakhsh himself: the celestial Soul, the Espahbad Light that moves its Heaven through the longing drawing it toward the Intellect from which it proceeds.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00690

The name “father,” repeated throughout the invocation, corresponds to its symbolic use among the Neoplatonists and in the Chaldean Oracles. It also suggests another reminiscence of the “Liturgy of Mithra.” Initiates who attained the highest rank in the mysteries of Mithra were called “fathers”; those at the rank immediately below them were the “sons” of these “fathers.” Their bond was far stronger than that between father and son by physical birth. It was a spiritual bond, for all were together the sons of Mithra, their “father.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00691

Under this name, and in this capacity, Mithra is invoked at the beginning of the Liturgy as the “father” who alone can impart—and can impart only to his “son”—what belongs to his own substance: that power (dynamis) whose birth or “initiation” within the human being is the sacramentum of the initiate's elevation to divine life. The final invocation of Suhrawardi's psalm aims at this same end. Suhrawardi will use the term “father” again in the Hermetically inspired psalm he addresses to his “Perfect Nature.” In the present psalm, the term reappears at every rank of the angelic hierarchy, joining all those ranks through a bond whose very name recalls the spiritual relationship uniting initiates in a brotherhood.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00692

Suhrawardi's psalm begins with a doxology, a hymn praising the beauties of the visible heavenly body, the luminous body of Lord Hûrakhsh. The invocation itself follows. Notice how it unfolds through an ascending series of mediators. It is addressed first to Lord Hûrakhsh; through him to the archangel Shahrîvar, whose theurgic manifestation is that luminous body; through Shahrîvar to all the Victorious Lights; through them to the primordial archangel Bahman; and through Bahman, finally, to the “Light of Lights,” the “God of Gods”—a term that also appears in the encyclopedia of the Brethren of Basra. This liturgical ascent corresponds to the “hieratic” ascent proposed by the Angel of initiation in several of Suhrawardi's visionary narratives. Here is the translation of the “Great Invocation to Hûrakhsh.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00693

“Blessed be the most luminous of beings endowed with life and thought, the most manifest of persons, the most radiant of heavenly bodies. Peace be upon you! May God's greetings and blessings rest upon you, sublime Luminary, most august of the wandering stars; you who obey the One who brought you into being, you who move through the ardor of love for the inaccessible majesty of your Creator.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00694

“You are Hûrakhsh the Mighty, Conqueror of Darkness, prince of Heaven, bringer of Day, by command of God Most High. You are king of the heavenly bodies, prince among the persons of the world above. By divine power and strength, which all obey, you reign over the Lights embodied in material forms. You are the body that dispenses Light, the Conqueror, the Radiant One, the Wise, the Supreme. In the incandescent splendor of your rays, you are the most magnificent of the children born of the spiritual world.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00695

“In the world of bodies, you are the vicegerent of the Light of Lights, who sets you ablaze with a Light that reaches the summit of its victory. You are an image of His greatness, a visible expression of His beauty, His sign before the eyes of His faithful. Glory to the One who gave you your form and your light, who made you a wanderer through burning desire for His inaccessible majesty, and who placed you in the fourth Heaven.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00696

“O most holy Father! I beg you to pray to the One who causes the splendor of your thinking soul to unfold at its East, the One who is your father, your cause, the object of your love, and the source of your motion—the One whose shadow and theurgic manifestation you are, the archangel Shahrîvar.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00697

“And I beg you to pray with him to all the Archangelic Lights, the immaterial Intellects, that they too may pray—in the manner of prayer proper to the eternal world, free from change and alteration—to the One who is their Father, their cause, and the object of their love: the most august of beings brought forth at the beginning, the Light nearest to the Principle, the Intellect of the universe, the archangel Bahman. May he, in the same manner, pray to his God, the God of Gods, the Eternally Subsisting, the Light of Lights, God of every Intellect, every Soul, every body of ether or of the elements, whether simple or compounded, the Necessary Being.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00698

“May he ask Him to illuminate my soul with flashes from the spiritual world, with knowledge of divine wisdom, and with the higher virtues. May he ask Him to count me among those who long for His Light, to protect me from every infirmity of soul and body, and to grant victory to the faithful of the Light and the mystical East. May He bless them and consecrate them, and us with them, for ever and ever. Amen.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00699

This psalm, so expressive of Suhrawardi's particular devotion and so faithful to the inspiration of “Eastern Theosophy,” contains a symbolism whose key may perhaps be found in the psalm to the “Perfect Nature.” Certainly this symbolism is bound up with a conception of the universe, an astronomy and a physics, that are no longer ours.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00700

Yet it seems scarcely necessary to point out that, at the deepest level of mystical consciousness, whether one accepts a geocentric or a heliocentric account of the heavens is beside the point. Both theories stand equally far from what is really at issue. Or, to use Suhrawardi's own word, each is only a “gateway” that must be crossed. And we know very well that no satellite, no Sputnik, no rocket of the future will ever be capable of passing through that gateway. For the force of gravity from which the soul, the inner human being, must free itself in order to cross it has nothing whatever to do with the gravity overcome by the forces, however extraordinary, discovered in the laboratories of our time.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00701

The ascending sequence of mediators invoked in the psalm suggests another observation. This liturgical progression presupposes a structure that we find in a strange dialogue. Its speakers are said to be the celebrated ninth-century Orthodox Christian physician Constantine, son of Luke (Qosta ibn Lûkâ), and his disciple ’Amâlaq the Greek, whose identity remains mysterious to us. Significantly, Ismaili theosophy seems to have adopted this dialogue, for we have found it in an Ismaili work that has not yet been published.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00702

We shall quote only a very short passage here. The disciple asks his master: “Will you not make my God known to me?” The master answers: “Do you know the one who makes you known to yourself [...] the one who frees you from sorrow, who brings forth within you something whose intimate sweetness you taste while also feeling its power, and who makes you independent of everything that is not himself? If you know that one, you can know him only as a part of yourself.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00703

“Then, yes, you have found your God; then you are a true believer.” When the disciple asks, “What lies beyond my God, so that I may be among those who have attained everything?” the sage replies: “Beyond him is the one who stands in relation to him as he himself stands in relation to you: one Unique to another Unique, and so onward until the threshold of the One in whom all the Uniques are contained.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00704

This dialogue opens up a “monadological” perspective—a vision of spiritual reality ordered through individual beings and their relationships—which belongs as much to Ismaili gnosis as to Ishrâqî theosophy. The sage's final words are in perfect harmony with what we hear at the end of several of Suhrawardi's narratives of initiation. His opening reply likewise implies what Suhrawardi calls the “Perfect Nature,” which the entire Ishrâqî tradition associates with the memory of Hermes' mystical experience. Since we cannot discuss Suhrawardi's entire “Book of Hours” here, or trace its connections with the Chaldean and Orphic devotion expressed in Neoplatonic hymns, or with the astral liturgies of the Hermetic Sabians of Harran, we shall at least give further attention to the psalm addressed to the “Perfect Nature.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00705

This psalm is addressed to the spiritual being whose name comes directly from Hermetic revelation as Suhrawardi and his school understood it: the “Perfect Nature” (al-Tibâ’ al-tâmm). We have already seen that this being is the philosopher's “Angel” (above, pp. 89 and 117), his tadaghât, in Arabic. In its own person it brings together the two meanings of the Xvarnah: it is both Light and the personal Destiny of the one whose “Angel” it is. Its significance for the soul's final destiny is already apparent in the fact that the ecstasy in which it sometimes reveals itself, as it revealed itself to Hermes, is a foretaste of the individual's ultimate spiritual fulfillment.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00706

We have already mentioned its presence even within Shiite teachings on the Imam. The commentators sometimes identify it with the Angel of humanity—Gabriel, the Holy Spirit—because it gives an individual form to that Angel's relationship with each human being. In every case, the Perfect Nature is what this Angel becomes for each person. And above that Angel there is another being who stands in relation to it as the Angel itself stands in relation to the human species. This is what we meant by a “monadological” perspective.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00707

In the preceding psalm, Suhrawardi asked the Angel of the Sun to ask all the Archangelic Lights to pray together to the First among them. Similarly, in his visionary narratives—for example, The Rustling of Gabriel's Wings and The Tale of the Western Exile—a mysterious figure appears, either at the beginning or later in the story. Referring to those who stand above him, he declares: “I am their tongue; beings like you cannot communicate with them.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00708

Likewise, in the writings of the Neoplatonist Proclus, there are Angels who serve as interpreters, revealing and explaining to human souls what would otherwise remain the Silence, the Unspoken reality of the Angels and gods belonging to the higher hierarchies. Anyone who impatiently claims to have no need of such mediators forgets a simple truth about experience itself. Whatever form the supreme divinity may take in appearing to someone, that form necessarily corresponds to the person's own manner of being.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00709

The divine cannot appear to that person in any way other than one suited to their capacity to receive and understand it. At the same time, the form reveals the limits of that capacity and, through the very act of its presence, points beyond those limits. This is the meaning of the Angel: what Suhrawardi expresses through the Angel of humanity, and what he himself experiences when the Perfect Nature appears to him.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00710

Here we should recall the original relationship that the shaykh al-Ishrâq places at the “dawn” of being, at the “East” from which all lights arise: the relationship between the first “beloved” and the first “lover.” Repeated at every level of existence, this relationship arranges the beings of every universe into pairs. It recurs between an Angel and the Species that is its “theurgic manifestation,” proceeding from its light. It recurs, too, wherever a being is joined by love to the heavenly cause from which it proceeds.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00711

Every being, our shaykh tells us, has a beloved in the higher world toward whom its longing is directed. This beloved mediates between it and the Being who exists by His own right (al-Haqq), and through this mediator it contemplates the divine Archangelic Lights. Suhrawardi therefore uses the word “father” here in an entirely symbolic sense, for the birth in question is the birth that the lover owes to the beloved. If the lover, precisely as a lover, owes his birth to the object of his love, this is because love reveals his own spiritual origin to him in the beloved, the higher being from whom he proceeds. The beloved is his higher “I,” whom he addresses as “you,” not an object about whom he speaks in the third person.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00712

Yet through this very revelation the lover, in turn, brings the beloved into being as beloved. This explains the striking reversibility of the terms, which we shall find in the very first words of the psalm below.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00713

“Among these Archangelic Lights that mediate the One who is Being in His own right (al-Haqq),” the shaykh writes in the Book of the Temples of Light, “there is one who stands toward us in the relationship of a ‘father.’ It is the archetype, the Lord of our Species, the Giver from whom our souls proceed. It is called the Holy Spirit; the philosophers call it the Active Intellect.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00714

In the Book of Eastern Theosophy, the shaykh explains further: “It is the Archangelic Light of which the thinking species is the theurgic manifestation: that is, the archangel Gabriel. It is the ‘father’ of the human race, the Near One among the supreme archangels of the Malakût, the Giver from whom our souls proceed (Ravân-bakhsh), the Holy Spirit (Rûh al-Qods), the Giver of knowledge and inspiring grace, the one who bestows life and excellence. From this Angel there emanates, upon the most perfect bodily constitution—the human constitution—an immaterial Light. This is the Light entrusted with the government of a human body, the Governing Light called the ‘Espahbad of human reality’ (Espahbad al-nâsût), the Light that refers to itself by saying ‘I’ (bi’l-anâ’ya).”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00715

Thus the tenth spiritual being of the Avicennian heavenly fullness is incorporated into the world of archetypal Lights described by Ishrâqî theosophy. More precisely, it belongs to the Latitudinal Order of the theurgic Angels, the archetypes of the Species, following the Zoroastrian archangels (Amahraspandân) named by Suhrawardi. It comes last because the radiance of all the preceding archetypal Lights converges within it, just as all the powers and radiations of the cosmos converge within the human microcosm.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00716

Suhrawardi's names for this being establish its identity: Holy Spirit, Angel Gabriel, Active Intellect. Particular emphasis should be placed on the purely Persian name Ravân-bakhsh, “the one from whom our souls proceed.” We have suggested elsewhere how this term may have originated in the Manichaean metaphysics of Light. Traditional Persian dictionaries merely confirm the meaning it came to have without explaining its origins: “It is the name of the Angel who possesses knowledge and wisdom; in Arabic, it is called the Holy Spirit.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00717

Suhrawardi gives the theme of the Ravân-bakhsh, the Giver of our souls, a striking visionary form at the beginning of one of his narratives of initiation. The Angel Gabriel, we are told, has two wings. The right wing, turned toward being, is pure and absolute light; from it our souls proceed. The left wing, turned toward non-being, bears a dark imprint, the shadow from which arises the world of mirage and illusion.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00718

There is more. This Angel, the Holy Spirit and Angel of humanity, is also identified with the Paraclete, and that identification is full of meaning. We have already recalled (above, Book I) how, in Shiism—for example, in the thought of Haydar Âmolî—the “Hidden Imam,” the “Expected Imam,” was also identified with the Paraclete.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00719

Once again we encounter the path that enables an eminent Shiite thinker such as Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî to see a correspondence between two relationships: that of the Archangelic Light called the Holy Spirit to each soul of light, and that of the Imam to each initiate, each soul left “orphaned” or “widowed” from the world of Light. Such convergences between the theosophy of Ishrâq and the theosophy of Shiism are characteristic of Iranian Islamic spirituality. Just as Haydar Âmolî explicitly refers to the Gospel of John, Suhrawardi quotes these words of Jesus: “I am going to my Father and your Father, so that He may send you the Paraclete, who will reveal to you the meaning of the symbols” (Gospel of John 14:16, 26).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00720
Finally, let us recall that in Suhrawardi's writings, the symbol of the dove of the Holy Spirit has its counterpart in the symbol of the sîmorgh (below, Chapter V).
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00721

As for the relationship between this Angel of humanity—the Holy Spirit or Paraclete—and the Perfect Nature, a relationship so close that one may take the place of the other, we shall try to clarify it later (Chapter VI) in connection with a visionary experience of Suhrawardi's. For now, let us say only that the Perfect Nature is to each human being what the Angel of humanity is to the human species as a whole. A being of light that exists before a person's earthly birth, it stands in such a relationship to that person that it is their protecting Angel, with whom they are finally reunited through death.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00722

Above all, however, it is significant that in Suhrawardi's teaching, every evocation of the Perfect Nature is associated with the name of Hermes. Suhrawardi recalls—and all the Ishrâqîyûn after him will recall—the vision Hermes describes in these words: “Then a being from the spiritual world inspired me—‘cast into me’—the higher forms of knowledge. I asked it: Who are you? It answered: I am your Perfect Nature.” Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî and others would frequently invoke this account. Elsewhere, too, the dangers Hermes faced during an ecstatic vision are recalled, dangers that caused him to cry out: “You who are my father, save me!”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00723

There is something in these accounts that recalls the Poimandres of the Corpus Hermeticum. Together with the parallels we have just noted, they enable us to understand the ardent, lyrical invocation found in Suhrawardi's “Book of Hours.” It follows the hymns or psalms he composed to be recited on each day of the week. Its title is Invocation (da’wat) to the Perfect Nature. Here is its translation:
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00724

“O You, my lord and prince, my most holy Angel, my precious spiritual being! You are the father who gave birth to me in the world of Spirit (ab rûhâni), and You are my child in the world of thought (walad ma’nawî). You are the one who, by divine permission, is devoted exclusively to the guidance of my person. You are the one whose fervent intercession before God, the God of Gods, makes up for all that I lack.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00725

“You who are clothed in the most radiant of divine Lights, You who dwell at the summit of the degrees of perfection, I implore You by the One who has filled You with such sublime nobility and poured out upon You such immeasurable grace. Ah, may You reveal Yourself to me in the supreme Epiphany! May You show me the light of Your dazzling Face! Be my mediator before the God of Gods in the outpouring of the light of the mystical Secrets. Remove from my heart the darkness of the veils. I beg this of You in the name of His rightful claim upon You and of His rank above You.”
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00726

It seems clear that the Mithraic ritual—the so-called “Liturgy of Mithra”—knows a spiritual situation corresponding to that expressed at the beginning of this psalm. There, too, the initiate experiences the opening of the “field of consciousness” belonging to the higher Self, the heavenly pole of the self, the Self addressed as “you,” which is the “father” of the earthly person.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00727

Yet although this higher, heavenly Self is our “father,” and although in one sense we are born from it, we must also, here below and in another sense, give birth to our higher Self if we are to establish any conscious relationship with it: a relationship between “I” and “you.” This, according to the Neoplatonic commentators on the Chaldean Oracles, is what it means to “act according to the archetype.” It is the fruit of the “theurgic” virtue that distinguishes initiates who have attained the highest spiritual rank. As anticipated above, The Tale of the Western Exile (below, Chapter VI) will give us occasion to bring together other texts concerning the Perfect Nature. Several sources of inspiration—Hermetic, Neoplatonic, Zoroastrian—can certainly be identified in Suhrawardi's thought.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00728

Yet they come together in his devotion to the “person” of the Perfect Nature, as that being is present to him and as he invokes it. And perhaps the entire mysticism of the “Faithful of Love” (below, Book III) is simply another way of reaching the manifestation of the Perfect Nature.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00729

We observed earlier that the decisive moment in the work—or, more precisely, in the inner life—of the shaykh al-Ishrâq comes when doctrine ceases trying to speak of the Ineffable and instead becomes an event. This is the moment when knowledge of divine wisdom and spiritual, “hieratic” experience come together.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00730

We now understand that it is because of this event that the mystical East gives its name to “Eastern” Theosophy. The event may take the form of a psalm in which the spiritual seeker addresses another as “you.” Or it may take the form of a narrative in which the seeker recounts, in the first person, an event experienced as happening to himself in the eighth clime, the imaginal world. Suhrawardi's visionary narratives form a cycle. When the protagonists of the event are heroes of the Iranian epic, as in the narrative translated later, they undergo an “Eastern” transformation. That is why what emerges above all in Suhrawardi's work is the passage from heroic epic to mystical epic (above, pp. 95, 102), a passage whose exemplary hero is King Kay Khosraw.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00731

Today we find ourselves trapped in a dilemma that seems to leave us no choice but between myth and history, or between the unconscious and rational consciousness. We have already suggested that this may be the result of a more or less agnostic understanding of being, one that can no longer recognize the real existence that properly belongs to the imaginal world, or distinguish that world from what is merely imaginary.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00732

In Suhrawardi's narratives, as in many accounts from the Shiite traditions, everything takes place on a level that rises above both sides of our false dilemma: neither myth nor history in the ordinary sense of those words. The same is true of the initiate's encounter with the Paraclete, or Perfect Nature. It is therefore all the more precious to recognize that the Iranian mystical epic crosses paths with the cycle in which the West may have deposited its deepest mystical secret, at a time when human beings had become incapable of bearing it: the cycle of the Holy Grail.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00733

We are dealing with something far more precise than similarities of folklore or recurring archetypes of the collective unconscious. We are dealing with shared “hieratic” Presences, with the Presence of a world common to both traditions. These Presences demand that the reality of their existence be fully acknowledged. This, of course, requires an understanding of being that has overcome the separation of thought from existence—a separation that so many minds in the West seem to find so difficult to abandon.
III. The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (Xvarnah) and Angelology
passage-en-00734

We have already alluded several times to the knighthood of the Grail when discussing the Shiite Imam and his faithful, and there will be further occasions to return to these connections. That something is shared, that there is a common Presence: this is among the most fascinating things the Iranian spiritual world can reveal to us. And it is no less significant that certain correspondences between the world of Iranian chivalry and that of Western mystical knighthood have been brought to light in our own time by a Zoroastrian scholar.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00735
Chapter IV The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
en-book-2-ch-4-s1
1. Hermetica and Mithriaca
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00736

The two Latin adjectives in this section's title refer to the spiritual treasures of two of humanity's great religious traditions: Hermeticism and Mithraism. I have brought them together because of two scholarly investigations. The more recent seeks the origins of the Western mystical understanding of the Holy Grail in the Corpus Hermeticum—more precisely, the understanding found in the German Grail cycle, in the work of Wolfram von Eschenbach.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00737

The earlier study seeks the origins of the Grail and its devoted knighthood in the Zoroastrian Xvarnah, the Light of Glory, and in the images and beliefs surrounding that Light. Neither an Ishrâqî—a follower of the philosophy of spiritual illumination—nor a scholar devoted to the tradition of Ishrâq can afford to overlook investigations of such exceptional interest.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00738

First, Suhrawardi's “Eastern theosophy,” which brings the ancient Persian world of light back to life while invoking Hermes and the Hermetic tradition, seems to us the ideal meeting place of these two lines of inquiry.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00739

Second, Suhrawardi's own understanding of what counts as evidence allows us to assess, from within the philosophy of illumination, the different degrees of credibility reached by the two investigations.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00740

We have already referred to the Grail, and to the role of its knights, on several occasions, and we shall return to them. They have arisen both in connection with Suhrawardi's revival of ancient Persian themes and in our discussion of the esoteric hierarchies of Twelver Shiism (Book I, Chapter III).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00741

We have also seen the idea of the Xvarnah appear in the triad of archangels belonging to Ismaili theosophy; in Suhrawardi it becomes explicit and fully conscious. To the shaykh al-Ishrâq, the master of illumination, the Xvarnah reveals itself as the very source of the mystical “East.” For him, the idea is inseparable from a hidden spiritual lineage: guardians of a secret treasure, headed by the being who is the mystical Pole of the world.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00742

In this company of companions, faithful through every trial, we recognise a recurring theme. In Zoroastrianism it is the band surrounding the Saoshyant, the Saviour who will appear at the close of the twelfth and final millennium of our Aeon and work with them to transfigure the world (frashkart). In Twelver Shiism it is the chosen companions of the presently hidden Twelfth Imam, who are even now preparing with him for the dawning of the Resurrection (Qiyâmat).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00743

We have also noticed echoes of Iranian chivalry when Suhrawardi calls the beings of Light who have descended into this world—the Zoroastrian Fravartis—the “Espahbad Lights of human reality,” or the commander-lights within the human being. Some among their elect are granted a vision of the sources of the Light of Glory. A modern Zoroastrian scholar has set out to demonstrate the proposition that this Light of Glory, the Xvarnah, and the Holy Grail are expressions of one and the same image.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00744

On the other hand, Hermes is, for Suhrawardi, the father of the sages and of all wisdom. Suhrawardi's Hermetic affinities are unmistakable, as is the kinship between certain of his psalms and the astral liturgies of the Sabians, who themselves revered Hermes and Agathodaimon.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00745

The visions of the Light of Glory experienced by Kay Khosraw and Zoroaster, and Hermes' sacred ascent to the world of Light “at the hour when the column of dawn bursts forth”—the hour of Ishrâq, of the mystical “East”—are two similar forms of the Event that fulfils the initiate's spiritual destiny: descent into this world, forgetfulness of one's origin, hearing the call, setting out upon the path of return, rebirth and final glorification. And the more recent of the two studies we shall discuss traces the spiritual meaning of the Holy Grail back to Hermeticism.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00746

The two investigations were carried out independently. The more recent scholars were unaware of the earlier Zoroastrian study, making it all the more interesting to compare their findings. Both, moreover, overlooked Suhrawardi's “Eastern theosophy” and the Iranian tradition that follows from it—the tradition he “resurrected”—which to us seems their natural meeting place.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00747

For within that tradition Hermes, Kay Khosraw and Zoroaster stand as equal heralds and guides into the mysteries of the same Light of Lights: the Light of Glory, which Suhrawardi names by its ancient Iranian name (Khorrah, Xvarnah), and in which the Zoroastrian scholar recognises an image identical to the Holy Grail. The studies matter profoundly to us for two reasons.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00748

First, the vision of this Light as a return or passage to the “East”—the initiate's goal—helps us understand that part of Suhrawardi's work in which philosophical teaching becomes a story of initiation.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00749

Second, it establishes a connection between Suhrawardi's tradition of Ishrâq and the Grail cycle, in which the West may have entrusted its deepest mystical secret. Through that connection, Suhrawardi's work, and with it a whole dimension of Iranian Islamic spirituality, comes unexpectedly close to us. The Grail leads us back to Hermeticism; the Iranian character of Suhrawardi's wisdom leads us back to the Grail. The circle closes, enclosing a vast spiritual realm: that of Ishrâq.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00750
These are the outlines of the circle that the two major studies allow us to draw. Their methods, and the rigour with which they apply them, differ.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00751

We shall consider them in reverse chronological order. The recent work is by two scholars at the University of Illinois, Henry and Renée Kahane. The other, some thirty years older, is by Sir Jahangir C. Coyajee, a Zoroastrian scholar in India.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00752

Unfortunately, it appeared on the eve of the Second World War in a journal with very limited circulation in France. These fascinating investigations invite a far longer discussion than we can offer here; we must be content with an outline. The Kahanes' study stands out for its painstaking comparison of the Corpus Hermeticum with Wolfram's Parzival, its deep knowledge of the Romance languages of the twelfth century, and its judicious scholarly caution. It suggests and proposes more than it asserts.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-00753

Indeed, its restraint may make it stronger, because it opens the way for further research. Our chief concern is with three questions: how the Kahanes believe Hermetic teachings reached the West and entered the Grail tradition; how they identify certain proper names whose distorted forms have long perplexed scholars; and how the climax of Wolfram's epic brings us to the very place where Suhrawardi leads the disciple of Ishrâq, the pilgrim of the “East.”
